units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. A big square, and a castle in the middle.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: This is what, a castle?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's called De Waag. It means the Weigh House.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And no, it's not a castle. It was built as a city gate.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A gate. Like a door in the wall.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. Its first name was Saint Anthony's Gate, the Sint Antoniespoort.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A stone on the building gives the date for the first stone as 28 April 1488.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One historian argues it might be older, around 1425, so the date may need correcting.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So we're not sure.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Sort of. That's the record. Slightly fuzzy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why's it not a gate now?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The city grew. By the late 16th century the wall had moved outward.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The gate was no longer on the edge.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1614, a stretch of canal beside it was filled in to make this square.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's why it's called the Nieuwmarkt.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The New Market.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the gate became a weigh house.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1617. Goods were weighed here, including anchors and artillery from the nearby shipyards.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, but you promised spooky.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I did. Look at the top floors.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Guilds had their halls up there.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Blacksmiths, painters, masons, and the surgeons.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Surgeons. Oh no.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The surgeons' guild had a lecture hall in the building.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's an inscription at their entrance.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Theatrum Anatomicum.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Anatomy theatre.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. Where bodies were dissected, in front of an audience.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In winter, I'm guessing. For the smell.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In winter, yes. According to the city's heritage site, the dissections were of the bodies of executed criminals.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the guild kept using the top floor for that until 1869.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Can we say something about the painting?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. Rembrandt's Anatomy Lesson of Doctor Nicolaes Tulp.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was painted in 1632. The surgeons' guild commissioned it, and each man in it paid to be included.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Pay to be in the picture. Very modern.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Quite. Now, we'll slow down a bit.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The corpse in the painting was a real person.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His name was Aris Kindt. He had been convicted of armed robbery and hanged earlier that day.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The dissection was on 31 January 1632.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Right.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The painting now hangs in the Mauritshuis, in The Hague.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not here. It was made for the guild.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's the record.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's the record.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the square itself? You said the city site had something to say.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It did. It says the Nieuwmarkt was known for corporal punishment and executions, though that source gives no dates.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in the first half of the 19th century, punishments were carried out in front of this building.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A guillotine was used here.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. That's a hard thing to stand on.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. That's not a ghost story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's documented. People suffered here.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So where's the legend?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We have to be honest. We didn't find a well-sourced ghost legend attached to the Waag.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There are plenty of internet claims about hauntings.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We can't back them up.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So we don't repeat them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We don't repeat them. You can stand here after dark and feel what you feel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But we won't tell you a ghost walks the roof.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fine. A clean stamp. Record, record, record.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Today the Waag has a cafe and restaurant on the ground floor, and a technology and society foundation above.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It became a national monument in 1970.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A restaurant in an old execution square.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. Cities do that.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Tally. Ghost stories, still nought.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Real history, two.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Don't gloat.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I'm deadpan. It's different.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Next?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Walk south-east, just a few minutes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A tall tower with a thin lead-covered spire rises over the rooftops.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Walk toward it. That's the Zuiderkerk.
